title: Missing the companies that died
objectives: Spot survivorship bias in a dataset of shares.
Build a point-in-time universe and keep dead firms with their delisting returns.

screens.title: Put the dead back
screens.prose: Our seeded market: 60 firms, monthly returns over 10 years. A firm whose price falls below 40% of its start is delisted the next month, with a delisting return of −50%. Slide through the months.
screens.question: At month 120, how much more is £100 worth in today's 45 than in all 60?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to month 120 and subtract the all-firms value from the survivors' value.

byKey.surv: That is the survivors' value alone. Subtract what all 60 firms gave.
byKey.all: That is what all 60 gave. Subtract it from the survivors' £367.24.

explain.text: The two lines start together and part as firms die: 60 listed in year 3, 46 by month 119. All 60, rebalanced each month and including each delisting loss, turn £100 into £207.00. Today's 45 turn it into £367.24, because they are, by construction, the ones that did not fail.

screens.title: Measure the bias
screens.prose: Judging a strategy only on firms that survived is **survivorship bias**, which you met in the probability course. Now measure it on the panel. `make_panel()` gives a table of monthly returns, one column per firm, with NaN after a firm dies.

state.caption: F48 is delisted in month 30 at −50%; from month 31 it is NaN.

screens.question: Complete `survivor_bias` so it returns the annualised mean return of the survivors and of all firms.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def make_panel(seed=5, n_firms=60, n_months=120, delist=-0.5, late=0):
    """Monthly returns of n_firms shares over n_months (rows: months, columns: firms).
    A firm whose price closes below 40% of its start is delisted the next month:
    that month's return is `delist`, and every later month is NaN.
    The last `late` firms list only from month 24 (NaN before)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mu = rng.normal(0.007, 0.006, n_firms)
    R = mu + 0.09 * rng.standard_normal((n_months, n_firms))
    R[:24, n_firms - late:] = np.nan
    for j in range(n_firms):
        p = 1.0
        for t in range(n_months):
            if np.isnan(R[t, j]):
                continue
            p *= 1 + R[t, j]
            if p < 0.4 and t + 1 < n_months:
                R[t + 1, j] = delist
                R[t + 2:, j] = np.nan
                break
    cols = [f"F{j + 1:02d}" for j in range(n_firms)]
    return pd.DataFrame(R, columns=cols)

widget.solution:
def survivor_bias(panel, alive_at_end):
    """panel: monthly returns, one column per firm, NaN
    after a firm dies. alive_at_end: firms listed in the
    last month. Returns 12 times the mean equal-weight
    monthly return of the survivors, then of all firms."""
    surv = panel[alive_at_end].mean(axis=1)
    everyone = panel.mean(axis=1)    # skips NaN
    return (round(float(12 * surv.mean()), 4),
            round(float(12 * everyone.mean()), 4))

import pandas as pd

def make_panel(seed=5, n_firms=60, n_months=120, delist=-0.5, late=0):
    """Monthly returns of n_firms shares over n_months (rows: months, columns: firms).
    A firm whose price closes below 40% of its start is delisted the next month:
    that month's return is `delist`, and every later month is NaN.
    The last `late` firms list only from month 24 (NaN before)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    mu = rng.normal(0.007, 0.006, n_firms)
    R = mu + 0.09 * rng.standard_normal((n_months, n_firms))
    R[:24, n_firms - late:] = np.nan
    for j in range(n_firms):
        p = 1.0
        for t in range(n_months):
            if np.isnan(R[t, j]):
                continue
            p *= 1 + R[t, j]
            if p < 0.4 and t + 1 < n_months:

widget.solution:
def dropna_kills(panel):
    """How many firms (columns) does keeping only
    full-history firms remove?"""
    full = panel.dropna(axis=1)
    return panel.shape[1] - full.shape[1]

screens.title: The universe as of a date
screens.prose: The fix starts with the universe. Store index membership as records, one per spell, and ask who was a member on each backtest date. Using today's top 100 by market value for a 2010 backtest is look-ahead: it picks 2010's future winners.
screens.question: Complete `universe_as_of` so it returns the members on `date`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests on the five records shown and an empty list. Each compares your sorted list with ==. Pure Python is enough: ISO dates compare correctly as strings.

hints.text: A firm is a member from its start date until the day before its end date.
Test `start <= date` and `end is None or date < end`.
`sorted(f for f, start, end in members if start <= date and (end is None or date < end))`.

feedback.correct: On 1 January 2010 the members were AAA and BBB.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Include the start date, exclude the end date, and treat `None` as still a member.

byKey.test-2: You kept BBB on 30 June 2012, the day it left. The end date is the first day it is no longer a member: use `date < end`.
byKey.test-4: You dropped firms on the day they joined. A firm is a member on its start date: use `start <= date`.

explain.text: On 1 January 2010 the members were AAA and BBB: DDD had left and CCC had not joined. A backtest built from today's list would hold CCC in 2010 and miss BBB. Point-in-time membership is what a backtest date could have known.

screens.title: When is there no bias?
screens.prose: Edge case. Market A lost no firms in 10 years. Market B lost 15 of 60 through mergers that happened at random, at the market price, unrelated to how the firms had done. In each, an analyst backtests today's members.
screens.question: Which backtests overstate the return of the whole market?

options.text: Only the one on our panel

options.why: You treated every exit as bias. In A nobody left, and in B leaving had nothing to do with returns.
In B the leavers were a random draw, so the stayers are a fair sample of the whole.
On our panel firms left because they fell; leaving them out lifted the return by 5.77 points a year.

hints.text: Does a survivor list differ from the whole when nobody leaves?
In market B, are the leavers any worse than the stayers?
Bias needs exits that depend on returns. Only our panel has them.

feedback.correct: Bias needs exits that depend on how firms did.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for each market, whether the firms that left did worse than those that stayed.

byKey.ab: In market B the leavers were picked at random, so the survivors are a fair sample. Random exits cost data, not accuracy.

explain.text: With no deaths the survivors are the whole market, so the bias is 0. With random exits they are a fair sample: less data, no bias. Our panel's deaths came from falling prices, which is how real delistings mostly happen.

screens.title: Dead, but with no loss
screens.prose: A colleague fixes the survivorship problem by keeping all 60 firms. The delisting returns were missing from the price file, so they filled them with 0. Their all-firm return is now 8.82% a year.
screens.question: How much of the 5.77-point bias is still in their number?

widget.label: Bias left, in percentage points a year

hints.text: Compare their number with the all-firm return that uses the actual delisting loss.
$8.82 - 7.40 = 1.42$ points a year are still missing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the 7.40% with real delisting losses from their 8.82%.

byKey.fixed: You took putting the firms back as the whole fix. A return of 0 says the holders lost nothing on the last day, when they lost half.
byKey.full: That is the whole bias before the fix. Their number already includes the dead firms' earlier months.
byKey.removed: That is the part they removed, 13.17% minus 8.82%. The question asks what is left.

explain.text: Setting the delisting return to 0 says shareholders walked away whole. In our panel they lost half, in the very month the firm left. Including dead firms fixes most of the bias; using their real delisting returns fixes the rest.

screens.title: A survivorship-free backtest
screens.prose: Put the fixes together. Each step closes one route by which the dead firms vanish.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: For each rebalance date, list the firms that were members on that date
Pull those firms' returns, dead firms included
Use the actual delisting return in the month a firm leaves
Average the returns of the firms held each month
Compound the monthly averages into the backtest

hints.text: What must you know before you can pull any returns?
The universe comes first: who was a member on each date.
Universe as of each date, then returns with dead firms, then delisting returns, then the average, then compounding.

feedback.correct: Universe, returns, delisting returns, average, compound.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from who was a member on each date and end with the compounded backtest.

byKey.r: Returns can only be pulled for a universe. List the members as of each date first.
byKey.c: Compounding comes last, once each month's average exists.

explain.text: The point-in-time universe stops look-ahead in the choice of firms. Keeping dead firms and their real delisting returns stops survivorship in the returns. The average and the compounding are then ordinary.

screens.title: The size of the gap
screens.prose: From the probability course: with survival $S$ and return $R$, $$E[R \mid S] - E[R] = P(S^c)\,\big(E[R \mid S] - E[R \mid S^c]\big).$$ The gap is the death rate times how much worse the dead did. It is 0 if nobody dies, or if dying is unrelated to returns.
screens.question: A fund database lists only open funds. Over ten years 30% of funds closed, after doing 4 points a year worse than the survivors. How far does the database overstate the average fund?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the share of funds that closed by how much worse they did.

byKey.four: That is how much worse the closed funds did. Only 30% of funds closed, so multiply by 0.30.

explain.text: $P(S^c) = 0.30$ and the gap in returns is 4 points, so the database overstates by $0.30 \times 4 = 1.2$ points a year. Studies of fund databases find premiums of the order of 1 to 2% a year: an order of magnitude, not a precise figure.

screens.title: Today's FTSE 100, from 2005
screens.prose: A backtest buys the shares in today's FTSE 100, in equal weights, from 2005. It beats the index itself by about 2% a year.

fell out, failed or were bought

screens.question: Why is the backtest's return too high?

options.text: It holds future joiners from 2005 and drops every share that fell out

options.why: Costs lower any backtest a little. They do not explain picking shares by what happened after 2005.
Weighting matters, but the index itself was not chosen with hindsight. The member list was.

options.text: It is not too high: large shares did well
options.why: You took the result at face value. The list of shares was chosen in 2025, using what happened after 2005.

hints.text: Which shares could a 2005 investor not have known to buy?
Shares join the FTSE 100 by rising and leave it by falling.
The backtest buys the future joiners early and never holds the leavers: look-ahead and survivorship together.

feedback.correct: The member list itself carries the future.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how today's list was chosen.

byKey.fine: You took the result at face value. Today's list was chosen with knowledge of what happened after 2005.

explain.text: Firms join the FTSE 100 by growing and leave it by shrinking, so today's list is a list of winners. Holding the joiners from 2005 is look-ahead; dropping the leavers is survivorship. Rebuild it from the membership as of each date.

ideas: A universe chosen today has no firms that went bust or were delisted, so its backtest looks better than any 2015 investor could have done.
On our panel of 60 firms, 15 deaths lifted the return from 7.40% to 13.17% a year; a filter like `dropna(axis=1)` does the same damage in one line.
Fix it with membership as of each date, dead firms kept, and their real delisting returns.

formula.name: Survivorship gap
formula.tex: E[R \mid S] - E[R] = P(S^c)\,\big(E[R \mid S] - E[R \mid S^c]\big)
formula.note: Zero with no deaths, or when deaths are unrelated to returns.

quiz.prose: Our panel has months as rows and firms as columns. The first firm to die is F48: its last return is in month 30. A colleague writes `panel.dropna()`, which drops rows.
quiz.question: What is left?

options.text: Months 0 to 30 only: 31 of the 120 months

options.why: That is `dropna(axis=1)`, which drops columns. Plain `dropna()` drops every row with any NaN.
The panel has NaN after each death, so `dropna()` has rows to drop.
Rows go from the first month with a NaN: month 31, the month after F48's last return.

feedback.correct: Every month after the first death has a NaN, so all of them go.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `dropna()` drops every row that contains any NaN.

explain.text: From month 31 on, F48 is NaN in every row, so `dropna()` drops months 31 to 120. Either direction of `dropna` on a panel with deaths quietly changes the question.

quiz.prose: Edge case. One of the 46 firms listed in the final month is delisted that month at −50%. A backtest leaves it out.
quiz.question: Roughly how much does that one omission lift the 10-year annualised mean return?

options.why: You applied the −50% to the whole portfolio. It is one firm of 46, in one month of 120.
One firm of 46 lifts that month by about 1.1%. Spread over 120 months, it is about a tenth of a point a year.

options.text: Nothing: it died on the last day
options.why: Its delisting loss is still part of the last month. Leaving it out does lift the result, a little.

feedback.correct: $0.5 / 46 \approx 1.1\%$ in one month, about 0.1 point a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One firm of 46, in one month of 120.

byKey.zero: Its −50% still belongs to the last month. Leaving it out lifts the result a little.

explain.text: Leaving it out lifts the last month's average by about $0.5/46 = 1.1\%$. Annualised as 12 times the mean of 120 months, that is about 0.1 point. A death on the last day costs little; deaths in the middle cost years of losses.

quiz.prose: Studies of fund databases put the survivorship premium at about 1 to 2% a year.
quiz.question: How should you use that figure?

options.text: As an order of magnitude for how much a survivor-only database flatters funds
Subtract exactly 1.5% from every fund's return
options.why: The premium varies by period, asset class and database. It is a size, not a correction to apply.

options.text: It applies only to failed funds
options.why: It is the gap in the average fund's return, caused by dropping the failed ones.
Many fund strategies earn 1% to 2% a year above their benchmark. The bias can be all of it.

feedback.correct: It tells you the size of the problem, not the exact fix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether 1 to 2% is a precise figure or a rough size.

byKey.subtract: The premium varies widely. Rebuild the database with dead funds instead.

explain.text: The figure says the bias is comparable to the edge most funds claim. The fix is a database that keeps dead funds, not a deduction.

quiz.prose: A desk's research wiki keeps a page for each signal that reached production: 12 signals, average live Sharpe 0.9. Signals that failed in testing were deleted.
quiz.question: What does the wiki overstate?

options.text: How often the desk's research produces a working signal

options.why: The live record of each kept signal is real. What is biased is the picture of the research process.
They never traded, but they were tried. Deleting them hides how many ideas it takes to find one.
Costs are a separate question. The wiki is missing the failures.

feedback.correct: A strategy archive can have survivorship bias too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is missing from the wiki.

byKey.nothing: Failed signals were still trials. Deleting them hides the real hit rate of research.

explain.text: With the failures deleted, the wiki suggests most ideas work. Keeping every trial, as Lesson 12's research log does, shows the true count.
